title: Customer Discovery Call - Harbor and Pine

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Hi Rachel, hi Jonas, thanks so much for making the time. I'm Alex, I lead product here, and Hannah from customer success is on as well. Is it okay if we record and take notes for the team?

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: Of course, that's fine. Nice to meet you both. I run retail operations at Harbor and Pine, and Jonas is our lead data analyst.

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: Hello. I mostly live in spreadsheets and our BI tool, so I'm curious about what you can do beyond that.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Great. We've been trying to understand how multi-store retailers actually track customers across channels, so mostly I want to listen. Could you walk us through how you look at customer behavior today?

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: So we have forty-two stores and an online shop. In stores we have a loyalty app, online we have the usual web analytics, and honestly those two worlds don't talk to each other. I can tell you what a customer bought online or what they bought in a store, but not how often the same person does both.

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: And it's mostly manual. Every Monday I export loyalty data, export the ecommerce orders, and try to match them on email address. About fifteen to twenty percent don't match because people use different emails.

segments.speaker: Hannah Schmidt
segments.text: That matching problem is pretty common with our retail customers. Do you know roughly how many of your customers shop both channels?

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: Our best guess is around nineteen percent, but it's a guess. If I had to bet, the real number is higher and those people spend a lot more.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: What do you do with that information when you get it? Who consumes the Monday report?

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: The merchandising team and the regional managers. The managers want to know which promotions are bringing people back. Right now they basically wait a month to see if a promotion worked.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: A month feels like forever. What would a good turnaround be?

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: Honestly, a week. If I knew within a week that the autumn loyalty bonus was working, I could extend it or kill it before we've burned the budget.

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: I'd say retention cohorts are the thing. How many customers who bought in September came back in October, split by store region and by whether they used a coupon.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: That's helpful. We do cohort retention, but I want to ask about the identity piece since you said emails don't match. If we could stitch the loyalty ID and the web customer ID together, would that be a deal breaker if it wasn't perfect?

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: Not a deal breaker, no. If we got to ninety percent matching I'd be thrilled. What worries me more is the data volume, we have about three million events a day in peak season.

segments.speaker: Hannah Schmidt
segments.text: Three million a day is well within what we handle. We have customers at ten times that. The more interesting question is where the data sits today.

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: Mostly in Snowflake. Our data team loads orders and loyalty events nightly. So we'd prefer something that reads from the warehouse rather than adding yet another tracking script.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: That's a really useful preference. We have a Snowflake connector, and we're about to ship a fix for timeouts on large warehouses, so that is timely. Does your warehouse have a lot of historical data?

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: Four years of orders. It's big. The last connector we tried choked on it.

segments.speaker: Hannah Schmidt
segments.text: We'd do a backfill in windows rather than pulling it all at once, so that shouldn't be an issue. I can walk Jonas through the approach separately.

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: Can I ask about price? We're not a huge company and I've been burned by tools that look cheap and then bill us by event.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Totally fair. Right now it's seat-based with a tracked user definition. We're actually rewriting the pricing page because people find it confusing, so your feedback is useful. What would feel fair to you?

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: Something predictable. A flat fee per month with a clear cap. I can explain a flat fee to my CFO, I can't explain an invoice that moves around.

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: And I'd want the whole analytics team to have access, not just two seats. If I'm the only person who can log in, nobody else benefits and it dies in a quarter.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: That makes sense, and it connects to something we hear from other customers. Per-seat pricing discourages sharing. We're discussing it internally, so I'll keep that in mind.

segments.speaker: Hannah Schmidt
segments.text: Hannah here, quickly, do you use Okta or something similar for login? Security usually gets involved.

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: We use Azure AD for everything. Our security team will absolutely require single sign-on before we put customer data into a new tool. That's a hard stop.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Good to know. SAML SSO for Azure AD is on our near-term list, we're scoping it now. I can't promise a date on this call, but it's targeted for early November.

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: Early November is okay if the pilot can start before that on a test environment without our real customer data.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: We can do that. A pilot with a sanitized sample from the warehouse, then expand once SSO is live. How would you measure whether the pilot worked?

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: If I could produce the Monday cohort report without touching a spreadsheet, that's a win. And if the regional managers can answer their own promotion questions without asking me.

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: And one more, the onboarding. Last tool took us two months to get value from. I need to see something useful in a couple of weeks or my team loses patience.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Onboarding is exactly what we're working on right now. We're redesigning the first-run experience so people see a working dashboard sooner. Hannah can be your dedicated contact during the pilot.

segments.speaker: Hannah Schmidt
segments.text: Happy to. I'd suggest a kickoff next week, a thirty minute technical session with Jonas on the Snowflake setup, and a check-in at two weeks.

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: That works for me. Can you send me a list of the tables and columns you'd need?

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Yes, Hannah will send a short data checklist today. Rachel, anything else you want us to think about before we wrap up?

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: Just one thing, a competitor pitched us last week with free implementation. If you can include some onboarding help in the pilot, that would go a long way.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Understood, I'll talk to our sales lead about what we can offer. I'll come back to you by Friday.

segments.speaker: Hannah Schmidt
segments.text: And I'll send the data checklist and a proposed kickoff time after the call.

segments.speaker: Jonas Weber
segments.text: Perfect. I'll talk to our data team about getting a sanitized sample ready.

segments.speaker: Rachel Kim
segments.text: Thanks both, this was useful. I'm cautiously optimistic.

segments.speaker: Alex Rivera
segments.text: Thank you both, this was really helpful for us too. Talk soon.

summary.overview: Alex and Hannah spoke with Rachel Kim and Jonas Weber of Harbor and Pine, a 42-store retailer, about how they analyze customer behavior. Their biggest pain is that loyalty app and ecommerce data cannot be matched, with 15 to 20 percent of customers failing to match by email, and a monthly lag before they learn whether promotions worked. They prefer a Snowflake-based approach, want predictable flat pricing with team-wide access, and require Azure AD single sign-on before any real data goes in. The team agreed to propose a pilot on sanitized data and to follow up on implementation help.
notes: Harbor and Pine runs 42 stores plus an online shop, and loyalty data and ecommerce data are not connected.
Weekly matching on email address fails for 15 to 20 percent of customers, so cross-channel behavior is largely guesswork.
Jonas estimates about 19 percent of customers shop both channels and expects the real number is higher.
Regional managers wait roughly a month to learn whether a promotion worked and want that cut to a week.
Their data lives in Snowflake with four years of orders and about 3 million events a day at peak.
Rachel wants predictable flat monthly pricing with a clear cap and warns that per-seat pricing would limit team adoption.
Azure AD single sign-on is a hard requirement from their security team before any customer data is loaded.
A pilot on a sanitized sample can start before SSO ships, which is targeted for early November.
Success means producing the Monday cohort report without spreadsheets and seeing value within about two weeks of onboarding.
